english: How many real roots does $F(\alpha,\beta,\gamma,x)=0$ have?
topic: Miscellaneous notes: a bound on the number of pairwise commuting infinitesimal projective transformations, a question on real roots of the hypergeometric function, a scheme for a space curve, a decision problem for integer solutions of Diophantine equations, and literature for a course on descriptive geometry.

triage.modern_statement: Take the Gauss hypergeometric function 2F1(α,β;γ;x) with real parameters α, β, γ. How many real zeros does it have, and how are they distributed among the intervals (0,1), (−∞,0) and (1,∞), as functions of the parameters? This includes the polynomial case α = −n, where the question becomes how many real zeros a Jacobi polynomial has.
triage.answered_by: Felix Klein, 'Über die Nullstellen der hypergeometrischen Reihe', Math. Ann. 37 (1890), 573–590, with a geometric proof. Adolf Hurwitz published on the same question the same year (Göttinger Nachrichten 1890, pp. 557–564; Math. Ann. 38 (1891), 452–458). For the polynomial (Jacobi) case, the resulting counts are known in the literature as the 'Hilbert–Klein formulas'. Later work includes Driver & Jordaan (arXiv 0812.0708), who re-derived Klein's results for F(−n,b;c;z) from results on Jacobi polynomials.

evidence.claim: Klein, 'Über die Nullstellen der hypergeometrischen Reihe', Math. Ann. 37 (1890) 573–590, is the standard reference for zeros of hypergeometric functions.

Hurwitz, 'Ueber die Nullstellen der hypergeometrischen Reihe', Nachr. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 1890, 557–564, and Math. Ann. 38 (1891), 452–458; Klein's Math. Ann. 37 paper is listed in the same bibliography.

The real zeros of F(−n,b;c;z) for real b and c are results due to Klein, who treated more general hypergeometric functions (not only polynomials) with a geometric proof that is hard to follow. The number of real zeros of Jacobi polynomials in the relevant intervals is given by the Hilbert–Klein formulas.
The number of real zeros of F(−n,b;c;z) for arbitrary real b and c, and the intervals where they lie, can be deduced from results for Jacobi polynomials.
Section 3 of this paper presents results originally due to Klein that give the number and location of real zeros of F(−n,b;c;z) for arbitrary real b and c.

triage.why: Hilbert's question matches the problem Klein solved in Math. Ann. 37 (1890), which Hurwitz also took up in 1890–91. The formulas for the polynomial case carry Hilbert's name alongside Klein's ('Hilbert–Klein formulas'), which suggests Hilbert worked on the case where the series terminates. The sources I found say so only through that name; I did not find Hilbert's own paper. Zeros of hypergeometric polynomials and functions are still studied, as the 2000s–2010s papers show. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Confidence is medium rather than high for two reasons: the diary note does not say which interval or which parameter range Hilbert meant, and I could not confirm the notebook's date relative to 1890.
